speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head W of the Estimates be reduced by $100." Mr Chairman, before I kick off the Committee of Supply (COS) Debate for the Ministry of Transport (MOT), I believe I speak for all Members of this House when I wish Minister Khaw Boon Wan a speedy recovery from his injury and we all look forward to the return of a formidable presence in this House very soon!

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Incidentally, Mr Chairman, as I cast my eyes across the floor, it suddenly dawned on me that with Minister Vivian Balakrishnan temporarily in-charge, the Ministry of Transport is now helmed by three doctors, all with a sub-specialty in children.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But, of course, we all agree that transport is no child's play.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I remember when I was appointed as the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) Chair for Transport in 2015, it was at a time when public satisfaction in our public transportation system and, in particular, the MRT system, was at one of its lowest points.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Being involved in GPC work for Transport then was quite a baptism of fire for me.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: On hindsight, it is understandable why public transportation is an issue close to the hearts of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Transportation is a key pillar and enabler of our economy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It connects us domestically within Singapore and also to the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is the first thing we plan for when we leave home in the morning and the last thing we rely on to bring us safely home each night.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In recent years, MOT has had to deal with the rapid evolution and the changing landscape of transportation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Advances in transport technology forces us to rethink and evolve the way we travel.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our domestic demographic and scarcity of land require us to adapt and constantly review our transportation system.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In order to do this, the Government continues to invest heavily in transportation infrastructure and also to push the transport industry to its technological forefront.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These include the rapid expansion and renewal of the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) system, the support of technological disruptions to the transportation industry, the proliferation of personal mobility devices (PMDs), e-bikes and bike sharing.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Other new technologies, such as driverless automated vehicles, are not far off on the horizon.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It has been a consistently increasing trend over the years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: With rapid changes however, difficulties and challenges will inevitably arise.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Some of these include the rail reliability of our MRT system, the disruption that private hire cars brought to the point-to-point (P2P) transportation market, safety issues between pedestrians and e-bikes and PMD users and even the irresponsible use and placement of shared bikes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These and other issues, when put together, often colour the public's perception of the efficiency and reliability of our entire transportation network.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In fairness, it is understandable how a new project or initiative, like the proliferation of e-bikes and PMDs, when viewed in isolation, can appear disjointed, or its challenges overwhelming.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This will require a seamless integration of public, active and shared transport networks that include enhanced infrastructure to support all modes of transportation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Viewed in the lens of the vision provided by LTMP 2040, the different projects and initiatives begin to complement one another better and the various pieces of the puzzle begin to fit together.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This bodes well for the future of transportation in Singapore and I am sure many of us are excited to see this vision realised.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There is still much work to be done, with more expansion and renewal work to be done to our MRT system in the pipeline.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But, for now, we can at least look forward to some stability in rail reliability as we continue to strive to improve.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This vision of building an inclusive, efficient and reliable domestic transport network, however, will come at a significant cost.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The ambitious targets outlined in LTMP 2040 will not come cheap.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: How will this cost burden affect the affordability of public transportation?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I hope that MOT can share with this House its plans on how it intends to manage these cost outlays efficiently and without an undue high cost burden on commuters.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Internationally, Singapore has traditionally been a trading port which used its strategic location in the region and excellent connectivity to the rest of the world to position itself as an aviation and maritime hub.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This not only contributed significantly to our Budget but also created many jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We have also added the Jewel to Changi Airport.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I must confess that before I visited the Jewel in early February this year, I had my doubts about the need for yet another shopping area at Changi Airport, given the shopping opportunities already available at the existing Terminals.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Instead, what I found when I visited the Jewel was a beautifully designed garden concept recreational centre which complements the existing Airport and exemplifies our position as a garden city.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It will also create many job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The Jewel will certainly be a delight for visitors and Singaporeans alike!

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We can be rightfully proud to be considered as one of the leading aviation and maritime hubs in the world.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: RTS will be a people-mover and it can significantly reduce the congestion at the Causeway and Second link.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Currently, thousands of commuters are stuck in the congestion daily.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The waste of time is causing losses in productivity.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With RTS, we will have less need for a third link.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, I would like to ask Acting Minister for Transport, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, how we can better engage Malaysia to shift the priority to RTS.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: What is the status of the RTS discussions now?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Meanwhile, I would like to wish Minister Khaw Boon Wan a speedy recovery.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With regard to Malaysia's dispute with Singapore over the port limits, it has been nearly five months since Malaysia decided to expand its port limits into Singapore's territories, which we disagree with.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: How would this affect the viability of our new Tuas port?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: What does it actually mean to us when waters within the port limits are not clearly defined?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: What impact would this have on Singapore’s maritime security in the short run and medium term?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With regard to Malaysia's dispute with Singapore over the usage of the Instrument Landing System (ILS), how would it affect the viability, safety or amount of air traffic which our new Seletar Airport can handle?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has been known internationally to manage its FIR efficiently and impartially.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With six airports, including international airports in Johor, Batam and Bintan within 50 nautical miles of Singapore, a fragmented FIR will raise the risk of mishaps and accidents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How does the Ministry currently manage flights bound for international airports in close proximity to Singapore, both inbound and outbound, and have our neighbours raised any issues with our management of the Singapore FIR thus far?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to seek an update on the Ministry's initiatives to better manage our airspace.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some years ago, a Centre of Excellence Air Traffic Management Fund of $200 million was set up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What has been the drawdown rate of this fund and what other measures has the Government lined up to ensure that Singapore maintains its status as a premier FIR manager?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What has been the Government's experience working together with the United Nations (UN) weather agency, the World Meteorological Organisation, since its establishment in Singapore in 2017 in benefiting the weather-sensitive aviation sector towards aviation safety?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This year’s Budget projects operating expenditure just above $2 billion, up from less than $1 billion a few years ago.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In 2017, the Public Transport Council (PTC) reported that 94.5% were satisfied with public transport, significantly up from earlier years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, I am concerned that efficiency has suffered even as quality has improved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Before GCM, bus operators generally had fare revenues within a few percentage points of operating costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Rail fare revenue was sufficient to cover operating costs, until recent years where losses have mounted due to maintenance expenditures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For the future, the Minister for Transport has said that fares may cover less than half of the operating expenses of the Thomson-East Coast Line.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, there is a difference between public transport operations and fully private transport markets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the private airline market, passengers buy the ticket that suits their needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Passengers do not buy Business Class if what they really want is Economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But in public transport, we make these decisions for commuters, using public funds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The good thing is, we can give all Singaporeans high-quality public transport even if the private market would not cater to them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we have to be careful that we do not overpay for services that are not valued by the commuting public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I urge the Ministry to outline a comprehensive strategy for ensuring we have both value for money and high quality in public transport operations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For buses, at the operational level, what can we do, using route design, schedule optimisation and new technology, such as on-demand services, to improve efficiency?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: On the strategic level, how are we evaluating the GCM and the contracting environment to improve competitiveness in tendering?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For rail, can we make further use of time of travel shifting measures, such as peak and off-peak fares, to reduce costly excess capacity?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Most importantly, how can we engage the fare-paying public to give them a role in determining what services they value and what they do not want to pay for?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since my Adjournment Motion speech on 15 January 2019, train delays are still taking place.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just yesterday, there was a train fault on Downtown Line during the morning rush hour.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, more can still be done to minimise train delays of any lengths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Ministry has been silent about keeping track of the many delays of not more than five minutes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Delays, whether long or short, have potential ripple effects that can snowball, meaning that these train delays affect other activities and constitute an economic cost to all involved.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore must continue to drive reliability even higher.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And as I have argued previously, we need to go beyond the current MKBF metrics in our reliability measurement approach.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Network Capacity Factor (NCF) continues to be of concern.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must also pay close attention to the impact of such fare hikes on vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to enhance service quality, including better punctuality for trains, as well as more accurate and timely displays of train delays.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also need to ensure better monitoring of service quality, including through independently measured service quality experience by customers that could be affected in the PTC's fare review formula, which is currently not the case.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current productivity extraction factors should be redefined to account for the PTO's profitability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Accounting for profitability will be more equitable for commuters.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Retail operations from operators will not be profitable without the infrastructure it operates in.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mandating the level of profits from retail operations to be added to the Railway Sinking Fund and the Rail Infrastructure Fund will move us towards a more equitable development of rail infrastructure in the long term.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Similar mechanisms can be done for bus infrastructure, too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most taxis and public buses are still running on diesel, and conversion to hybrid or electric options will still take quite a few more years for taxis and an even longer time for buses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The short-term rebates will likely not be enough to stop operators passing the costs to consumers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since the Government did not push for the conversion to start earlier, it should give more reasonable timelines for bus and taxi companies to convert to hybrid or electric options fully before applying the tax increase.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Government truly believes in environmental conservation, it should attend more to the electric vehicle and charging stations availability side of the equation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps that is the longer-term approach that Singapore can take to mitigate environmental concerns.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Tuas South is currently being developed for existing and new businesses.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses, such as the Tuas Mega Port, shipbuilding industry, Biomedical Park, electronics firms, logistic and cold chain companies, petrochemical companies, among others.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: These are mainly companies with decent pay, decent work environment and some even utilising state-of-the-art technologies.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: These are good jobs, jobs which we want Singaporeans to be gainfully employed in.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: The challenge is: how do we attract Singaporeans to go there to work?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: I recall that in our early years of industrialisation, the Government faced the same but different challenges.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Enticing Singaporeans to take up employment in the Jurong Industrial Estate was also no easy feat despite high unemployment then.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Besides building public housing in Jurong, one of the things done then was to develop a public transport system to facilitate Singaporeans from other parts of the country to commute to work daily.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the comprehensive shuttle and trunk services, in addition to company-provided transport.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: As it is, the area is rather remote to most Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: In terms of accessibility, Malaysian workers have it better, compared to the locals, due to the proximity of the Tuas Second link.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: The nearest MRT station is Tuas West station.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Taking a train from Ang Mo Kio to Tuas West Station, the travelling time is about 65 minutes, not factoring in the time taken to travel from home to station and station to the work area.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: The duration is by no means short for the workers who have to commute daily.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Such long distances will deter Singaporeans staying in the northern, eastern and central areas from wanting to work in Tuas South.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: I understand employers had a hard time getting local Singaporeans to work in the Tuas area.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: With the companies providing transport, the situation was slightly better, and it improved with the opening of the Tuas West extension line.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: I encountered a similar situation when the port moved to Pasir Panjang, and the workers had some challenge when transferred to the new terminals, till the opening of the Circle Line.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Readily available public transport, especially our MRT train services, is a critical factor to be considered to facilitate Singaporeans to work in the Tuas South area, notably when the area is being developed to provide good employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: While businesses might provide transport for their workers, not all might do so.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans will use other means to travel to work in order to save time, and this poses a risk, especially travelling long distances after completing the graveyard shift.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: If LTA aims to ensure the maximum of 45 minutes of travelling time between one’s home and work at Shenton Way, I do not see why the Government cannot consider it for workers working in an area where the future of work is.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: There is no denying that the cost of building and operating an MRT line will be high and there is always an issue of ridership, at least till the place is fully developed and bustling with activities.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, I humbly believe it is a chicken-and-egg problem.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Without easy accessibility to an efficient public transport, Singaporeans will find it challenging to take up employment in Tuas South.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses will find it difficult to expand or gear up their activities due to human resource constraints.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the ridership may not reach the so-called optimal number.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Surely when we first embarked on industrialisation in Jurong Town, ridership was not the top priority or consideration when developing the transport system.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: It was about providing a public transport service to facilitate Singaporeans seeking employment in Jurong.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: For the same reason, I urge the Government to continue to do likewise and ensure every Singaporean who takes up employment in the Tuas South area can do so with a safe, comfortable and efficient transport service.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: It is not only about the companies and businesses in Tuas South.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: It is about every worker and “Every Worker Matters”.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Low Yen Ling, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Ministry constantly seeks to better understand commuters and plan our transport systems for future needs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Recently, it released LTMP 2040 which had sought more than 7,000 views from the public on what they valued in their travel.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: According to the surveys, commuters prized convenience most, followed by connectivity and fast travel time.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Proximity to bus stops and MRT stations, as well as ease of transferring from one transport mode to another also featured prominently in the feedback.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In line with this, the Advisory Panel for the Master Plan made these recommendations: (a) to offer commuters more public, active and shared modes of transport; (b) to develop a more inclusive transport system for families, elderly and persons with disabilities; and (c) to create journeys for healthier lifestyles and a more liveable Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We welcome all these goals and hope that the aims of LTMP 2040 will translate to a change in status for the currently underserved Hume area.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Without an MRT station, the Master Plan can only be a dream for the residents staying in and around Hume.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This distance of 2.6 km is more than double the average 1.1 km found between most train stations.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Each time a Hume resident wants to take the Downtown Line, it entails a detour backwards to Hillview or to Beauty World, or a squeeze onto the crowded buses at peak hours.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, to get to Hillview MRT station, Hume residents need to "backtrack" in their bus routes, and peak hour travel could mean longer waiting times.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Residents heading to town via Beauty World MRT station are often subject to an extended wait because most buses plying Upper Bukit Timah Road are full by the time they reach Bukit Gombak.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Residents could spend 15 minutes or more before being able to squeeze up a bus, and this really means that the vision of a 45-minute city is really beyond their reach.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I would like to strongly urge MOT/LTA not to leave Hume out of the new Master Plan.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Build the MRT station now at Hume, so that the residents there can have a chance to be part of the new transport goals.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With an MRT station at Hume, residents will be placed on track the new Master Plan.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With seamless multi-modes of transport, their travel times will be reduced.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Children and elderly residents, as well as residents with disabilities, would be able to enjoy safer travels with an inclusive train transport system, right from their estate.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Constructing the Hume MRT station will create journeys that promote healthier lifestyles – one objective of the new Master Plan – and a more liveable Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is a key objective of the Master Plan.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A new MRT station in Hume will certainly bring the people closer to the planned Rail Corridor.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The development has historical significance and plenty of recreational potential.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It has eight distinctively-themed stretches along its 24-km long Corridor and 10 community nodes offering differentiated experiences.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, I was very heartened to hear Minister Desmond Lee's update during the MND COS yesterday to know that the former Bukit Timah Fire Station will be developed into a visitor centre and a recreational node.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have been broaching on the ground in Bukit Gombak with MND and the Urban Redevelopment Authority on this possibility and I am very happy that Minister Desmond Lee shared that this will come to fruition in the former Bukit Timah Fire Station soon.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Now, by providing access to the historical site, Hume MRT station will strengthen the residents' sense of local identity and enhance Singaporeans' appreciation of our past in that belt.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, we hope that the Ministry will see different possibilities that an MRT station in Hume can offer.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Today, rail stations have the potential to become destinations and lifestyle centres that blend commuting with exercise, community with recreation, and actually community with even understanding history.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: People are increasingly using stations not just as a transport node, but also as places for leisure and social activities.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, the iconic New York Grand Central Terminal and London’s St Pancras Station are crowd pleasers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They draw a lot of traffic to those stations with their history, architecture, shopping and also dining choices.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the Rail Corridor in its backyard, Hume MRT station can eventually evolve into an exciting node promoting healthy lifestyles and a highly liveable Bukit Gombak in the South West District.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, as I have illustrated, we have a strong and also a compelling case for building Hume MRT station.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I strongly urge MOT and LTA to consider making investments in transportation that have widespread benefits.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When transport systems are efficient and underserved, gaps are being closed, they can provide social and economic opportunities that lead to positive multiplier effects in that area, for example, higher footfall or even tourism, new businesses, and also healthier and better lifestyles.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Conversely, when transport systems are lacking, they lead to reduced or missed opportunities and can lead to a lower quality of life.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, like many urban cities, we constantly face the challenges of growing transport needs and development, as well as physical space constraints on our island-state.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Bukit Gombak, we have benefited from MOT and LTA's plan to create a people-centred transport system in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since the Downtown Line started a few years back, our residents' travelling time into the city has been reduced significantly.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The provision of covered walkways around our constituency has enhanced our journeys and last-mile connection.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, some of the residents said they leave their cars at home and take the train during the weekday to work.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I wish to register my heartfelt appreciation and gratitude to MOT and LTA for their hard work and patience in listening to all our transport requests.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The numerous site visits and discussions have, indeed, resulted in improving the commuting experience in Bukit Gombak.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Through the years, we have improved our roads and walkways, as well as introduced new bus services.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, residents staying on the opposite side of Hillview Avenue, from Hillview Peak all the way to Hillview Crescent, they are feeling the heat, especially now, in their commute to the bus stop or as they walk up to Hillview MRT station.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We hope LTA would consider extending the last-mile connection to these residents with the construction of a sheltered walkway.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a result of this change in bus service, residents no longer have a direct link to Chua Chu Kang MRT station and bus interchange, as well as important amenities like the Choa Chu Kang Polyclinic, Teck Whye Shopping Centre and nearby markets.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This situation can be changed if LTA could review the service 991 bus route to meet these unmet needs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We would like to request LTA, please close the gap with a sheltered walkway to serve these Keat Hong Axis and Colors residents.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thirdly, we hope that the Ministry will continue to look into transport enhancement for Bukit Gombak as our town grows in size and network.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Bukit Gombak is no stranger to the Ministry of Defence.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is home to many army personnel at the Gombak camp and we are glad that the upcoming NS Hub in our vicinity will serve our NSmen as well.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While we look forward to the arrival of NS Hub in four years' time, we are also mindful of the transport considerations as more traffic, people and movement are anticipated to come into Bukit Gombak.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As I had highlighted in my COS speech on transport in the last few years, a crucial transport link is needed to connect the Hillview area and the Bukit Gombak Neighbourhood Centre.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Currently, residents from the Bukit Gombak Neighbourbood Centre who want to use the Downtown Line MRT station, although it is just about one km away, they would have to take two buses to get to the Hillview MRT station.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is the same situation if they wish to get to our newly completed Community Club (CC), or if they wish to shop at the fairly new HillV2 mall.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Having to change buses adds precious minutes to their travelling and waiting time within the constituency.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Likewise, residents staying at the Hillview area do not have a direct bus to the Bukit Gombak Neighbourhood Centre that has more than 10 coffee shops and more than 108 Housing and Development Board (HDB) shops for them to do their marketing and also buying of groceries.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This lack of community coverage and connection within the constituency actually draws an invisible line across our estate that has several "centres of gravity" or hubs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Without direct bus coverage, the flow of movement, the flow of people between the two sides of Bukit Gombak is somewhat hampered.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A direct bus link would offer greater chances for our residents, especially from the largely private estate of Hillview, to go to Bukit Gombak Neighbourhood Centre where the markets, HDB estate and shops are, and vice versa, for residents staying at the Bukit Gombak area to easily access HillV2 mall and also to enjoy the facilities at our Hillview CC.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As the node for our constituency activities and events, the CC should be made easily accessible to all our residents, especially residents who rely on public transport.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, Chairman, we need a people-centred transport system for community bonding and integration in our estate.

speaker: The Chairman
text: You may take your next three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Last year, I urged MOT to consider nurturing local expertise to build and maintain the MRT system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: A good comparison is Hong Kong Mass Transit Railway.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Hong Kong has acquired sufficient expertise in building, maintaining and operating their train system so much so that they are winning a lot of contracts overseas.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In many countries, large Government projects typically have offset obligation of a certain percentage, some as high as 50%, to require the foreign contractor to partner and allocate works to local companies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Very often, such a scheme also involves knowledge transfers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I am not advocating imposing offset obligation immediately.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: However, could we not move in this direction?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: As part of the evaluation criteria for awarding large MRT contracts, I hope LTA can consider mandating the tenderers to showcase their plan to better engage local contractors and facilitate technology transfers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The Panel for LTMP 2040 envisioned that Singaporeans would be able to reach neighbourhood towns within 20 minutes, and the city within 45 minutes, by 2040.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: And this appears very great, but 2040 appears quite far away.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I suppose rail network will be the cornerstone, the backbone and pillar of LTMP 2040.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Thus, why can we not reach the vision of 45-Minute City by 2030?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: What will be the additional significant improvements to land transport that MOT is thinking about between 2030 and 2040?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: How many Singaporeans can now travel to the city within 45 minutes?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: How many households are now staying within a 10-minute walk of a train station?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: For people who are staying within a 10-minute walk from the train station near their home and their workplace is also within a 10-minute walk to a train station, what is the current, average and median and 90th percentile of travelling time to the city?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: If not, what are the obstacles that are preventing them from doing so?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: With this reality check, there can be a better understanding of the current constraints that both MOT and Singaporeans can work together to reach the 2040 vision.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: If there are obstacles, we need to remove the obstacles together.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: If we need to change the mindset to better embrace public transport and shared transportation, let us work out the strategy together.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I would first like to declare my interest as the chief executive officer of ComfortDelGro's taxi business.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In the past few years, the P2P transport sector has been heavily disrupted by new players, new technology and new money.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The recent PTC survey showed that consumers had no clear preference between private hire cars and taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: This shows that both sectors are serving largely the same group of people.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In the last few years, the authority has adopted a wait-and-see approach pertaining to the ride hailing sector.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: At the same time, the authority continues to regulate the taxi sector as tight as before and this has created some distortions and disruptions to the market.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Before the entry of private hire cars, we have 28,000 taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: But this number is not enough to meet the peak hour demand, especially during rainy days.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: And that is why commuters are experiencing surge pricing, which can be a few times the taxi metered fare during peak hours.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: During off-peak, there are then too many vehicles for hire.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In an era of no regulation for the ride hailing sector, the ride hailing company is buying market share by subsidising fare through generous promotion codes – burning money, burning investors' money.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Drivers are also happy because they are getting generous incentives from the ride hailing company and these incentives can be more than the fares they collected.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In recent days, we can also see that a player unilaterally imposing cancellation charges and location surcharge without the need of obtaining approval from the authority.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: So, this is the case of winner takes all.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In the short run, commuters cheer the promotion codes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: A certain party also urges the taxi drivers to drive for the ride hailing company to enjoy the incentives.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In the long run, when one winner takes all, it will be bad for both the commuters and the drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: And this is why the authorities see the need to intervene in the P2P transport sector.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I would suggest three areas where we need to pay more attention.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: During peak hours, it is widely reported that surge pricing can be a few times the taxi metered fare.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: On the contrary, very low peak hour fares will also drive the supply away.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Today, ride hailing companies claim that their cater rate can be almost 100%.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: And this is because when you ask for private car, and it can come to you but it could be 20 minutes or more.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: So, what should be the acceptable definition of vehicle availability?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: This is where the public and commuters need to be consulted.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Safety is important and I hope that the authorities can take that into consideration.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, I would like to declare my interest as the union representative for the private hire drivers as well as the taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Commuters have more choices and more workers have become vocational drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have previously called for a review of the regulations for private hire and taxi operators to first better safeguard interests of commuters; second, ensure fair competition; and third, offer better welfare for the drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An example was the initial partnership of Uber and ComfortDelGro (CDG) and a subsequent merger of Uber and Grab in 2018.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Drivers must be allowed to choose jobs from any platforms or arrangements.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should, therefore, avoid situations where operators cause unnecessary anxiety among drivers by telling them that they will not cover drivers' insurance if anything happens while they fetch passengers using another service platform.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should also avoid operators working together to co-share commission and end up competing less with one another.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Decisions by operators have a big impact on consumers' options and drivers' livelihood.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, operators can unilaterally decide to ban or suspend drivers according to their own rules.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As drivers are self-employed, the Employment Act does not apply to them and they have limited recourse.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We propose that the Ministry form tripartite workgroups to agree on hiring terms, among other issues to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is in tandem with the Ministry of Manpower's (MOM's) proposed recommendations for Self-Employed Persons (SEPs).

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, we already have such a tripartite workgroup for taxi drivers, taxi operators and LTA.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ride-hailing operators also have light assets, making it easy for them to suddenly exit to the detriment of drivers, commuters and their own employees.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The sudden exit of Uber was a case in point.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ride-hailing operators also collect monies on behalf of drivers and any delay in payments will not be fair to the drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, the new licensure should ensure that there are safeguards, such as security deposits or minimum payment periods, by the operators.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, the P2P sector also includes the traditional limousine drivers and others who belong to informal networks.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have met many of them throughout the last few years.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many operate on varying degrees of matching and driving as a service.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Drivers, so called, "page out" jobs from their regular clients to other members when they are unable to fulfil them.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Drivers in this group have expressed serious concerns if the regulations are onerous.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The authority had taken a light-touch regulatory approach for foreign new entrants like Uber and Grab for several years.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Look how far these operators have come and how much they have benefited.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should, therefore, provide similar leeway to our local groups to operate alongside these bigwigs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It appears that too many drivers are fighting for a limited pie.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should we consider capping the number of such vehicles?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should we not have more modes of leasing like hourly rental?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should the age of new taxi and private hire drivers not be raised to prevent an over-supply situation?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The members of the associations have met with Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary on the proposed recommendations and we will continue to have such dialogues with him to ensure that our commuters and drivers will be safeguarded.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Chairman, the market for urban mobility has changed significantly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Innovations, such as private hire ride hailing and bicycle sharing, have made commuting easier and faster.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: At the same time, there have been growing pains, ranging from market dominance in ride-hailing, to indiscriminate parking of shared bicycles, and unrecoverable debts from failed startups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The Government's light-touch approach has helped these markets grow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But at times, the locus of regulation has been unclear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: PTC, meanwhile, has no statutory authority over ride-hailing and PMD services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: What are the Ministry's plans to design more integrated and holistic regulation for urban mobility services?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Such services are part of the broader public transport ecosystem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Many operators see the potential for vertical integration of services from public transport, to P2P to PMDs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: To achieve the LTMP 2040 target of nine in 10 journeys using public, active, and shared modes of transport, regulation should take a broader view.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Further, could the PTC's statutory authority be widened to serve as a one-stop shop to safeguard the interests of commuters and stakeholders in the broader public transport ecosystem?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Melvin Yong, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, technological advances will allow us to reinvent and reimagine our land transport system.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One good example is the introduction of on-demand public buses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The intention of such a trial is to evaluate the feasibility of operating public bus service with routes and schedules based on real-time commuter demand instead of following current fixed routes and predetermined timetables.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I recently visited Shenton Way Bus Terminal to learn how the trial at Marina Downtown area has been progressing and to also talk to our bus workers operating the service.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: From what I observed, there are clear benefits to this system.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: By being more responsive to the real-time changes in commuter demand, we can reduce empty mileage quite significantly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, the trial operates only during off-peak hours.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to suggest for the system to incorporate the use of virtual bus stops.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With technology, we can increase convenience for commuters by allowing them to select their pickup and drop-off points along certain designated zones instead of confining to current traditional bus stops.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that the Ministry can consider extending the ODPB trial to the Dunearn and Bukit Timah estates which are currently located within my constituency.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are many elderly residents living in these areas, and having such a service would be useful for those who may find that the nearest bus stop or MRT station is quite a distance to walk.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of the bus captains I spoke to shared that they were not able to adapt well to the rigours of being always on demand.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They preferred to work on fixed and scheduled routes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I, therefore, urge the Ministry to also consider drivers' stress, drivers' fatigue and work with the union and the public transport operators to look after the needs of our bus drivers who are plying on such ODPBs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I sit on the LTMP Advisory Panel and we have recently announced our recommendations on LTMP 2040.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Harnessing technology will be key to realising some of the recommendations made by the panel.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, the flipside of harnessing that very same technology will have the potential disruptions to the livelihoods of many of our public transport workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Here, I declare my interest as the executive secretary of the National Transport Workers' Union (NTWU), and I would like to ask the Ministry to shed more light on the impact of the LTMP 2040 recommendations on public transport workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there plans to ensure that our public transport workers are ready to embrace artificial intelligence (AI) and digitalisation?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The union stands ready to work with the Ministry and the transport operators to help our workers keep up with technology changes and ensure that they are well-prepared to handle future challenges in this sector, but we need the Government's support for this.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One key technology that Singapore has been exploring in recent years is the use of autonomous vehicles (AVs).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are several ongoing trials for AVs, including autonomous buses, with the most recent being the Nanyang Technological University's (NTU's) collaboration with Volvo to test self-driving electric buses in actual traffic conditions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At a recent focus group discussion where Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng were also present, our public transport workers and union leaders expressed strong concerns over the uncertainty of their jobs due to the impending adoption of autonomous buses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, I have also raised these concerns at every COS since 2017.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, as we move towards a car-lite society, the Government needs to ensure that our public transport is reliable, efficient, extensively connected and cost-effective.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, residents often complain of pathways being unsafe because of the different devices on it, and parents and grandparents still feel that they cannot hold the hands of the children as it is not safe.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is safe for the children to walk in front of them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry share on their enforcement actions, such as staff strength, to make our pathways safer?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Last year, an SBST bus collided with an SMRT bus along Jalan Jurong Kechil, leaving 33 people injured and LTA released a statement emphasising that safety is of paramount important.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, at last year's COS, many Members of Parliament spoke up about the dangers caused by speeding e-scooters and indiscriminate parking by users of bike-sharing services.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A year is a long time for bike sharing firms.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While bike-sharing companies had contributed much to disamenities, they have also played an important role in terms of last-mile connectivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Mr Chairman, I agree with Mr Sitoh Yih Pin wholeheartedly that the work of the Transport Ministry is no child's play.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: It affects the lives of thousands and millions of Singaporeans on a daily basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Speaking as a pediatric ophthalmologist, and I believe my fellow pediatric colleagues will agree that besides treating or operating on a patient who is a child, what is most important is to win the confidence and trust of the parents who put the lives and well-being of their precious ones in our hands.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Similarly, as we aspire to make our public transport system world-class, we need to gain the confidence and trust of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: For example, Singaporeans have made personal sacrifices, such as during the early closures and late openings while we step up maintenance and upgrading works for the rail system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: I want to thank Singaporeans for their understanding.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We must not rest on our laurels, and we will continue to work hard at it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Mr Chairman, may I have your permission for slides to be displayed during MOT's replies to Members?

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Chairman, Members have raised good questions about MOT's work across air, sea and land transport.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Together, Acting Minister for Transport Vivian Balakrishnan, Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng and I will address the queries in three themes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Changi Airport and our port play an important role in making Singapore a global city and a vibrant economic hub.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For this theme, I will speak on how we are strengthening connectivity with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and working with international organisations, as well as investing in our air and sea hubs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In addition to discussing domestic public transport issues, Acting Minister for Transport Vivian Balakrishnan will also address Members' questions on bilateral issues with Malaysia.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Second, Cultivating Innovation and Creating Opportunities for All.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Embracing technology and innovation will be key in strengthening our transport sectors and creating opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I will share on some technologies we are harnessing in the aviation and maritime domains.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Back home, we are embracing innovative commuting options, such as private hire cars and active mobility devices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will speak on our plans to regulate the P2P sector, and I will speak on active mobility.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Last year, we started work on the next LTMP to set out the vision for our land transport system in 2040.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have consulted widely to co-create a vision with Singaporeans and build a land transport system which meets the diverse needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will elaborate on LTMP 2040 and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng will share how we are creating an inclusive land transport system for all.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But even before 1819, there were already records of Singapore being a thriving seaport.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We were a location where East meets West and, for many centuries, an important port for trading valuable spices like pepper and nutmeg.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: After Independence, our Pioneers turned our location into an advantage.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: They built the first container terminal in Southeast Asia at Tanjong Pagar in 1972, despite the uncertainty that containerisation would even take off.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Not long after, against the consultants' recommendations, they shifted our international airport from Paya Lebar to Changi, to accommodate the future expansion of the airport.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Today, our buzzing seaport and Changi Airport are all part and parcel of the Singapore identity.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But we cannot take what we have for granted.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As Mr Sitoh Yih Pin rightly noted, there is much to be done for our air and sea hubs to remain relevant and competitive in the long term.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The flow of goods and people is dependent on good connectivity between different regions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: A dense network of Southeast Asia nodes will enable all of us to ride on Asia's growth together.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This has coincided with a period of strong growth in ASEAN tourism.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The expansion of connectivity beyond ASEAN will further stimulate tourism growth.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Singapore's extensive air links to China also connect Chinese passengers to the region.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Singapore/Malaysia/Thailand tour itinerary (新马泰游) is a popular one.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Singapore Tourism Board, Changi Airport Group and Royal Caribbean International also have a tripartite partnership to sail Chinese Fly-Cruise tourists from Singapore to Southeast Asia.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is why Singapore participates actively in establishing stronger links between the region and the rest of the world.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There are ongoing negotiations on air transport agreements between ASEAN and the European Union, and between ASEAN and Japan.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These agreements would further boost economic ties and enable the aviation industries of these countries to better tap on the Asia Pacific market.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Similarly, maritime connectivity plays an important role in supporting the growing region.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Over the past decade, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development has recorded a steady rise in the Liner Shipping Connectivity Index scores of ASEAN countries.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This means that the region is increasingly connected to the global shipping network.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have built a reliable and densely connected network, by anchoring key shipping lines and alliances that ply the main shipping route from Asia to Europe.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Together with our strong complementary feeder network to ASEAN ports, we ensure that goods manufactured in Southeast Asia can be delivered efficiently worldwide.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are also developing new and efficient maritime trade routes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This new route helps businesses in Southeast Asia access Chinese markets more efficiently.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, Indonesian paper pulp is traditionally shipped via bulk to Jiangsu and conveyed by barge into Chongqing.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Now, they can be containerised and transported through the CCI-ILSTC, saving time and money for businesses.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Chairman, we must also grow our connectivity in a sustainable way.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In this regard, Singapore contributes actively to the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and International Maritime Organization (IMO), to play our part in strengthening international aviation and maritime systems.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This global initiative will help ICAO achieve its aspirational goal of carbon-neutral growth from 2020.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the same time, we are working with ASEAN to push for our collective interest at international platforms.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The idea is to identify areas where species would be naturally transferred without using ballast water from ships as a medium and thus regarded as having the "same risk".

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Ships operating in the "Same Risk Area" can then be exempted from IMO's requirement to install ballast water management systems.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This makes it easier for ships operating short voyages in our region, while ensuring that we play our part in protecting the marine environment.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Back home, we must continue to invest in quality infrastructure to provide the needed capacity and strengthen Singapore's global connectivity.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are currently building Tuas Terminal and developing Changi East, including the new Terminal 5 (T5).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Chairman, with your permission, I would like to display some photos on the LED screens.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Not only will Tuas Terminal be able to handle high container volumes and bigger vessels, but it will be a smarter port with a higher degree of automation to improve efficiency, safety and service levels.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Similarly, the development of Changi East is on track and T5 is expected to commence operations around 2030.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Before T5 comes on stream, we will enhance our current airport infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Jewel will also open on 17 April, with aviation facilities that will improve the travel experience for passengers, such as early check-in facilities, integrated ticketing and baggage services for fly-cruise and fly-coach transfers, in addition to its array of attractions and retail and dining offerings.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: And I guess he must be referring to popular food and beverage brands like American fastfood chain, Shake Shack, London's famed Burger and Lobster chain, the Merdeka Generation's old favourite A&W, and local delights like Violet Onn's restaurant.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I had the privilege to go on a sneak preview of Jewel together with Mr Sitoh Yih Pin and my first impression was "Wow!".

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Indeed, it will live up to its name "Jewel" and be a world-class lifestyle destination set to inspire and entertain visitors, both local and overseas.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Upgrading works on Terminal 2 will also start soon.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Terminal 2 will be expanded and refreshed, with automated check-in kiosks, biometric-enabled bag drops and automated immigration gates, to offer passengers greater convenience from check-in to immigration to their flight.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Harnessing technology and innovation is one of our main strategies under the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) for both air and sea transport.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since the ITMs were rolled out early last year, we have been working closely with the industry and unions to review systems and processes and use technology to augment human capabilities.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the airport, airside drivers drive tractors to tow baggage between terminals and aircraft.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: So, with support from the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS), the Singapore Airport Terminal Services (SATS), the largest ground handler at Changi, is experimenting with Autonomous Container Trailers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If successful, it would mean less physically straining jobs, and more higher-skilled jobs, such as Autonomous Vehicle Operators and Fleet Managers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are also automating our seaport to raise productivity.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Jurong Port previously used traditional forklifts and flatbed trailers to unload steel, which constitutes more than half of their handled cargo.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It now deploys customised sideloaders which have helped to reduce its manpower requirement for steel unloading by 60%.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Such technologies make a real difference to our port workers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: One of them is Mr Haja Maidin, who has worked as a Container Equipment Specialist at PSA for the past 27 years.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The automation of yard cranes at Pasir Panjang Terminal gave Mr Haja the opportunity to take on a supervisory role as a Ground Operations Controller.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: He also picked up new skills to use stowage planning systems.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Besides investing in technology, we want to help our companies embrace technology.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The idea is to make going digital simple for SMEs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The IDP provides a step-by-step guide on digital technologies that SMEs can adopt at different stages of growth.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: SMEs can also tap on available Government co-funding when they adopt the list of digital solutions relevant for the sea transport sector for their digital journey.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As a start, we will be rolling out the Sea Transport IDP to ship agencies and harbour craft companies.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: More details will be provided at the Sea Transport IDP launch.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will also continue to experiment and push the boundaries of emerging technology.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked about the Centre of Excellence for Air Traffic Management.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Pritam Singh also asked for the status of our space-based VHF communications for air traffic management.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Globally, space-based VHF communications technology is still nascent and still under development.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: CAAS is in the design phase together with our industry partners.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But it is important that we help our companies build deep capabilities today, so that they gain competitive advantages for the future.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Several companies are already taking a lead in building that "innovator’s DNA" in their workforce.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Singapore Airlines and Lufthansa have opened their own innovation labs in Singapore to trial new technologies.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Wärtsilä, a Finnish maritime company, has also set up their Digital Acceleration Centre as part of MPA’s Living Lab initiative.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to create a supportive environment and explore deeper collaborations with the industry.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: One area is unmanned aircraft systems, more commonly referred to as drones.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Its close proximity to an anchorage provides a conducive environment to testbed and develop drone technology for maritime applications.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It will also serve as a regulatory sandbox for the development of regulatory and safety standards for maritime drone operations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The industry has already been active in this arena.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, Wilhelmsen and Airbus are trialling the use of drones to deliver goods from shore to ship, which will increase productivity and reduce manpower needed, compared to deliveries by boats today.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As we facilitate more beneficial uses of drones, we are mindful of the potential safety and security threats arising from its errant and irresponsible use, as seen from the incidents at Gatwick and Newark airports.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In January, I had informed the House that we have in place measures to deal with such threats and coordinate very closely with the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Home Affairs on such efforts.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Chairman, our aviation and maritime investments will create rewarding career opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Businesses are participating in Workforce Singapore’s career fairs to recruit locals into these jobs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Our efforts to attract global players to grow their businesses in Singapore will also create more job and business opportunities.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Last year, we welcomed new entrants into our maritime sector, such as Thenemaris and Cheng Lie Navigation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Key players already in Singapore, such as Ocean Network Express, Wilhelmsen Ship Management and Wärtsilä, have also expanded their operations here.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the same time, under the ITMs, the Government, unions and companies are working together to develop a future-ready aviation and maritime workforce.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Some workers may worry about how their current jobs will be affected by technological changes and whether their skillsets will remain relevant for the future.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I want to assure them that we will support them to grow and learn new skills.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: CAAS and SkillsFuture Singapore, in consultation with the tripartite partners, launched the Skills Framework for the Air Transport Sector last year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It informs employees of career pathways and the skills required for different jobs and provides companies with guidelines for better employee training.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: More aviation companies are using the framework to invest in the training and development of their employees.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, SATS has set up a SATS Academy which introduces interesting ways of staff training, such as using virtual reality to simulate scenarios for technical ramp training.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are also better integrating studies and work.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We already have several programmes that allow students and employees to work and study at the same time.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: One such programme is MPA’s Global Internship Award (GIA) which allows students to intern at international maritime companies, whilst still pursuing their undergraduate studies.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Damon Er interned at Braemar ACM Shipbroking under the GIA in 2016 when he was still studying at NTU.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: He received a job offer right after the internship and is now working as a dry cargo Capesize trainee broker.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have received good feedback on the Earn-and-Learn Programme (ELP) which allows fresh graduates to work and obtain an industry-recognised certification at the same time.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Elias Heng started his career under the ELP for Marine Engineering Officer and sailed as a Fourth Engineer with Apex Ship Management Pte Ltd.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The structured on-the-job training helped him prepare for higher seafaring certifications.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Upon completion of ELP, he went on to further his training and has since been promoted to a Third Engineer with Apex.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Likewise, Ms Kylie Pang, a SATS customer services agent, pursued two skills-based Modular Certificates under ELP which helped her develop both soft and technical skills.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This gave her a headstart in her career.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With these enhancements, more people will benefit from ELP, just like Elias and Kylie.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Chairman, Minister Khaw Boon Wan has asked me to convey his apologies for missing COS.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I can assure all Members that he is recovering well after surgery and, in fact, has been following the debate assiduously.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Many of these incidents occur at home, usually at night or early morning.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, as a doctor, I can tell you the most vulnerable moments are those few seconds or minutes when you wake up from and get out of bed.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We all want a public transport system that is safe, reliable, convenient and affordable.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Four worthy objectives, but sometimes you have to make some tough choices and tradeoffs.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Bear these words in mind: safe, reliable, convenient, affordable.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our transport system is actually in a very strong position.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: That is thanks to many generations of visionary leaders, meticulous planners and, of course, the transport workers themselves who work long hours.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They wake up way before everyone else has woken up and they also work into the wee hours of the night to maintain and operate our bus and rail networks.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are expanding our MRT network which, after all, is the backbone of our public transport system.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Over the last five years, we completed the Downtown Line and Tuas West Extension, and we added close to 50 km to our network.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will open the first phase of our sixth MRT line – the Thomson-East Coast Line (TEL) by the end of this year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: By around 2030, we can look forward to the opening of the Circle Line Stage 6, the Jurong Region Line and the Cross Island Line.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: When all these new lines come onstream, we will achieve our target of having eight in 10 households within a 10-minute walk from a train station.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We added 200 trains over the last five years.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We also introduced 1,000 buses under the Bus Service Enhancement Programme, and this was completed in 2017.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are conducting trials with on-demand buses and cleaner, greener vehicles.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have also added 500 km of road lanes over the last 10 years and are building more.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But this is, as Minister Khaw has emphasised in the past, a multi-year effort.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: He has also said that we are not out of the woods yet.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will continue to work on improving rail reliability.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, we have to continue to work on this.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are also renewing and enhancing the Bukit Panjang LRT (BPLRT), which now requires new trains, resignalling and power rail system enhancements.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: With these efforts, we hope BPLRT will also become a lot more reliable in the future, and I must confess that I have a personal stake in this, as one of the local Members of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The independent PTC tracks this through the annual Public Transport Customer Satisfaction Survey.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I think Assoc Prof Walter Theseira referred to this in his speech.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The mean satisfaction score went up to 7.9 in 2018, which is the highest level since we started measuring in 2008.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: LTA embarked on its most extensive public engagement exercise thus far for LTMP 2040.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are grateful to the more than 7,000 Singaporeans who have contributed ideas to this plan.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The LTMP Advisory Panel, which is chaired by Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary, has worked very hard to take all these views into account and submitted its recommendations to the Government on 15 February 2019.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Panel appreciated that a transport system does not just convey people to a place.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
